L'Herutano et les autres artisans magiques

L'Herutano emploie le Mentalisme. Ses enchantements reposent sur une maîtrise approfondie de l'esprit et sur l'interaction de ses pouvoirs avec les objets.

Le Razak-Zinul appartient aux traditions des Khazâd et pratique la Théurgie. Ses connaissances concernent particulièrement les ouvrages, les inscriptions et les méthodes artisanales de son peuple.

L'Alchimiste est un utilisateur d'Essence, dont les Listes offrent une formation plus générale dans les transformations et les enchantements.

Ces professions peuvent poursuivre des objectifs semblables, mais leurs royaumes de magie, leurs traditions et leurs Listes demeurent distincts.

Le fëa et l'art des Eldar

L'association entre le fëa et la matière permet de représenter, dans les mécanismes de MERP-RMU, la relation particulière des Elfes avec leurs créations.

Elle constitue une interprétation ludique et ne doit pas être présentée comme une explication exhaustive de la magie elfique chez Tolkien.

Les Herutanor ne disposent d'aucun pouvoir général leur permettant de partager, de fragmenter ou de transférer leur âme dans des objets.

Les œuvres exceptionnelles

Les Silmarils, les Anneaux de Pouvoir et les autres grandes œuvres de Tolkien appartiennent à des événements uniques de l'histoire d'Arda.

Ils constituent des références littéraires pour représenter les traditions des artisans, mais ne doivent pas être assimilés à des objets qu'un personnage pourrait réaliser automatiquement en développant une Liste de sorts.

Le Meneur conserve ainsi la distinction entre les créations accessibles aux personnages selon RMU et les œuvres exceptionnelles dont la nature dépasse les mécanismes ordinaires du jeu.

Ombre et Corruption

La profession ne possède aucune association intrinsèque avec l'Ombre.

Les risques apparaissent lorsque le personnage emploie des pouvoirs corrompus, recherche une domination injustifiée ou accepte des enseignements dont la nature relève des mécanismes d'Ombre et de Corruption prévus par MERP-RMU.

L'histoire de Fëanor et celle des artisans d'Eregion offrent des références importantes pour développer les thèmes de l'orgueil, de la convoitise et de la tentation de préserver les choses au prix de la liberté d'autrui.

Le Meneur doit toutefois distinguer les fautes morales ordinaires des événements qui entraînent effectivement des conséquences mécaniques de Corruption.

L'Herutano prend toute sa dimension lorsqu'il est incarné comme un maître artisan dont la maîtrise de la matière, la discipline intérieure et le sens des responsabilités déterminent la nature des œuvres qu'il laissera derrière lui.

Herutano

The Art of the Eldar, Between Matter and Will

In the last years of Eregion, the workshops of Ost-in-Edhil remain among the most renowned in Middle-earth. There, craftsmen work precious metals, stone, gems, and substances whose properties have been studied over many long centuries. Merchants from Lindon regularly pass through the city, while the Dwarves of Khazad-dûm bring their ores, their creations, and the knowledge their masters are willing to share.

In a room opening onto an inner courtyard, an Elf examines a small silver piece resting on a cushion of dark cloth. Several tools lie before her: engraving instruments, fine tongs, abrasive stones, and a lamp whose light falls directly upon her workbench.

The Elf is named Eleneth. She belongs to a family of Noldor who left the western lands many generations ago. Her master once taught her the arts of engraving and cutting stone, before gradually introducing her to the more complex disciplines that make it possible to imbue crafted objects with particular magical properties.

For several days, she has been working on a clasp intended for a travelling cloak.

The patron is an Elf whose duties regularly take him along the roads between Eregion and the neighbouring settlements. He wants a sturdy fastening that can withstand long journeys and inclement weather. But Eleneth has also undertaken to give it a special property: the clasp should help protect the garment from the strains to which it will be exposed, through an enchantment she already knows.

Her apprentice, a young Sinda named Lethion, brings her a strip of metal prepared that morning. He studies the clasp and notices that its inscriptions are nearly complete.

“The piece looks finished,” he says.

Eleneth turns it slowly between her fingers.

“The characters are correct. The work still needs to be tested.”

She asks him to bring several pieces of cloth and an old cloak kept in the workshop. Then she fastens the clasp to the garment and begins a series of tests. The metal holds firm, but a slight deformation appears when one of the fastenings is pulled.

The mistress removes the clasp and examines the weak point.

The flaw is almost invisible. Her apprentice would probably never have noticed it had she not shown him.

“We shall rework this part,” she explains. “A creation intended to protect its wearer must first withstand the ordinary stresses to which it will be subjected.”

Lethion nods. For several years, he has been learning that enchantment demands a mastery of materials every bit as rigorous as the magical disciplines themselves.

A little later, a visitor enters the workshop.

He is a craftsman from Khazad-dûm whom the mistress has known for many years. He carries a small wooden box reinforced with metal fittings. Inside lies a fragment of dark stone, its surface bearing several deeply engraved characters.

The Dwarf explains that the stone once formed part of a mechanism fitted to an ancient door. The workers who found it want to know whether it still retains a particular property, since its inscriptions differ from those ordinarily used in their halls.

Eleneth examines the fragment and then places it under a brighter light.

The signs belong to a tradition she knows only imperfectly. Some characters seem to come from an ancient script; others were added later by a less skilful hand.

She also recognises traces of a magical alteration.

The Dwarf asks whether she could restore the inscription.

Eleneth hesitates.

She possesses the knowledge needed to examine certain powers imbedded in matter, but the origin of this enchantment remains uncertain. The signs have been altered, and nothing yet reveals the purpose of the construction to which they belonged.

She explains her reservations to her visitor.

“I can study the stone and investigate the nature of what remains within it. Restoring it will require more. We shall need to recover the other fragments and understand what the door was used for.”

The Dwarf agrees. He would rather preserve an incomplete work than alter its properties through an ill-prepared intervention.

They agree to continue the examination once the other pieces have been brought from Khazad-dûm.

After he leaves, Lethion questions his mistress.

“If we manage to identify the enchantment, why must we wait?”

Eleneth carefully replaces the fragment in its box.

“Because we still know too little about the one who created it. An object may retain its power long after its purpose has been forgotten. Before using it, we must understand what it did and why it was made.”

The young Elf gazes at the inscriptions.

Since coming to the workshop, he has discovered works that once seemed impossible to him. He has seen metals retain extraordinary properties, gems receive enchantments, and ancient objects reveal knowledge left behind by their creators.

He now understands that such mastery requires as much judgement as skill.

The years to come will bring him many other lessons. He will learn to recognise the effects of an unknown power, prepare his own enchantments, and maintain the concentration required to unite his intention with the matter he works.

But the events approaching will transform his life profoundly.

Sauron has already presented himself in Eregion under a deceptive guise, and the teachings he has brought to the craftsmen have paved the way for the creation of the Rings of Power. When his true intentions are discovered, the realm of the smiths will be drawn into a war from which few of its great works will emerge intact.

Eleneth and her apprentice will then have to decide which works to preserve, what knowledge to pass on, and which creations to abandon in order to save those who depend upon them.

They belong to the Herutanor, those Elven craftsmen whose mastery of matter is inseparable from a profound discipline of the mind.

Their art makes it possible to create extraordinary objects. Their responsibility is also to understand what they will pass on to the generations that follow.

Heirs to the Great Craftsmen

Among the Eldar, the arts of creation hold a remarkable place. The Elves possess a profound affinity for the beauty of form, precision of workmanship, and the knowledge that allows natural materials to be transformed into enduring creations. Their longevity gives them time to refine techniques over periods exceeding the entire lifetime of many human craftsmen.

The Herutano, a term presented in MERP material as meaning “master craftsman,” belongs to this tradition. In the plural, the Herutanor are practitioners whose knowledge combines craftsmanship with the disciplines of Mentalism.

Their training rests on a thorough mastery of materials, accompanied by a particular ability to focus their will and direct their inner power towards the works they create. Some fashion enchanted weapons or protective equipment; others work gems, natural substances, or objects whose properties exceed those of their ordinary materials.

Among the Elves, craftsmanship remains closely bound to the history of their peoples. The Noldor preserve the traditions of the workshops of Valinor and Beleriand, while the Sindar possess their own knowledge of materials, forms, and works suited to their dwellings. The craftsmen of the woodland realms develop other practices, often involving wood, plants, and the substances found in their surroundings.

These traditions can meet and enrich one another. A Noldo dwelling among the Sindar discovers methods unknown to his first masters; a craftsman from the western lands studies under a Khazâd whose experience of metal and stone is exceptionally deep.

The Herutano may therefore belong to different Elven cultures, subject to the restrictions established by MERP-UI. Their origins determine the materials they know, the objects they hold precious, and the teachings to which they may have gained access.

Years of Training

The apprenticeship begins with a rigorous knowledge of ordinary materials. The young Elf learns to work wood, stone, or metal according to the traditions of their master. They observe variations in texture, flaws that undermine the strength of an object, and the techniques required to achieve a precise shape.

Such training requires considerable patience. A gem must be studied before it is cut, since certain inclusions may cause it to fracture. Working metal requires an understanding of how it reacts to heat, while joining different materials demands knowledge of the stresses each places upon the others.

The first creations are generally modest. The apprentice produces pieces whose quality is carefully assessed, then is entrusted with increasingly complex work. They also learn to repair ancient creations, an activity that reveals methods different from those they use themselves.

Magical instruction begins once these skills are sufficiently established. The master teaches the disciple to gather their attention, maintain a clear intention, and employ the powers of Mentalism to act upon matter.

This inner discipline may take several years before yielding truly controlled results. The first experiments involve limited effects performed upon objects whose properties are thoroughly understood. The difficulty increases when the craftsman undertakes to transform more complex materials or fix lasting enchantments within them.

Training also includes the study of ancient works. A Herutano must be able to recognise methods used by their predecessors and determine what distinguishes an exceptional object from an ordinary creation. This knowledge becomes particularly important when they discover works whose masters disappeared several Ages ago.

Apprentices are often encouraged to develop a speciality, but their training remains broad enough to let them understand the work of other craftsmen. One who favours gem engraving must understand the properties of metal settings; one who fashions weapons must understand the demands of their use.

True mastery emerges when these branches of knowledge complement one another and the practitioner can undertake a work from the selection of its materials to its magical completion.

The Fëa and the Creative Will

The Elves possess a particular relationship between their spirit, the fëa, and their body, the hröa. Their nature allows them to develop faculties in which thought, intention, and bodily action remain profoundly connected.

Within MERP-RMU, this conception provides a foundation for the Herutano's magic. Their powers belong to Mentalism, and their effects upon matter are represented as the result of an interaction between the practitioner's inner discipline and the object being worked.

The craftsman learns to direct their attention with remarkable precision. They must understand the desired form, the properties of the material, and the consequences of the magical effect they wish to produce. Hesitation may jeopardise a delicate operation, particularly when several transformations must be coordinated.

Years of training enable them to maintain this concentration throughout demanding tasks. Some masters can pursue their research over long periods, alternating meditation, examination of materials, and magical operations themselves.

This inner mastery also has personal applications. Certain Herutano spell lists allow the practitioner to act upon their own body, preserve their faculties, or contribute to their healing. The connection between mental discipline and bodily functions thus becomes an important aspect of their training.

An essential distinction from Tolkien's cosmology must nevertheless be maintained. The Herutano does not literally detach a part of their soul to imprison it within a gem or weapon. The language of imbedding refers here to the game's magical mechanics and to the way a creator's intention can be associated with an object's properties.

The craftsman must also accept the limits of their powers. Profound concentration does not allow them to disregard the nature of materials, and the effects they achieve remain those of the spells they actually know.

The Workshops of Valinor and Beleriand

The craft traditions of the Noldor reach an extraordinary level of development during their sojourn in Aman. Under Aulë, they acquire profound knowledge of materials and methods of manufacture. Their workshops become places where masters devote long years to discovering new forms and improving techniques already remarkable in their own right.

Fëanor, son of Finwë, remains the most celebrated figure of this tradition. His skill surpasses that of the other craftsmen of his people, and his researches lead, above all, to the creation of the Silmarils, which preserve the light of the Two Trees.

This work belongs among the most extraordinary events in the history of Arda. Its creation is a unique achievement, whose nature and significance lie beyond the ordinary powers available to player characters.

Fëanor's fate, however, reveals the dangers that can accompany exceptional mastery. His attachment to the Silmarils, the pride that increasingly shapes his decisions, and the oaths sworn after Morgoth steals them have tragic consequences for the Noldor.

In the First Age, the realms of Beleriand maintain other traditions. In Gondolin, craftsmen produce weapons, protective equipment, and works, some of which will survive the city's destruction. Among the objects associated with this history are the blades found much later in the Trolls' lair and carried during the Quest of Erebor.

These creations bear witness to the remarkable endurance of Elven works. They may lie unused for centuries before finding a place once more in the events of the world.

A Herutano of the First Age may have trained under the Noldor who returned from Aman or belong to a tradition developed among the Elves of Middle-earth. Their knowledge is then deeply shaped by the great wars, migrations, and gradual disappearance of the realms of Beleriand.

Eregion and the Teachings of Annatar

In the Second Age, Eregion becomes one of the leading centres of Elven craftsmanship. Its proximity to Khazad-dûm encourages especially close relations between the Noldor and the Khazâd, whose craftsmen exchange materials, techniques, and knowledge.

The Gwaith-i-Mírdain, the jewel-smiths, achieve an exceptional reputation under the leadership of Celebrimbor.

Their workshops bring together masters whose researches concern precious metals, gems, and the powers that may be imparted to certain creations. Knowledge inherited from their predecessors is deepened through contact with Dwarven methods, and the resulting works display a mastery seldom equalled since the days of Fëanor.

It is in this setting that Sauron, disguised under the name Annatar, presents himself to the Elven craftsmen.

He offers teachings that promise to increase their abilities immeasurably. The knowledge he imparts enables the creation of the Rings of Power, but also forms part of a design for domination whose full significance the craftsmen do not immediately perceive.

When Sauron forges the One Ring in Mordor, his intentions are revealed. The craftsmen of Eregion then discover the danger to which their research has exposed them.

The war that follows brings about the destruction of the realm in S.A. 1697. Celebrimbor perishes, the workshops are laid waste, and much of the knowledge accumulated over several centuries disappears with its masters.

For a Herutano, this history carries an essential meaning. It shows how promises of knowledge can entice creators who sincerely cherish the beauty and preservation of their works.

A craftsman may wish to protect a dwelling against the passage of time, preserve a garden whose every tree they know, or fashion an object capable of keeping a precious memory alive. Yet the means offered to achieve these ends may bind them to obligations whose consequences they do not at first understand.

The history of Eregion thus offers an especially rich setting for characters whose apprenticeship was interrupted by war or who have inherited manuscripts from the lost workshops.

The Art of Creating and Preserving

The Herutano's disciplines encompass several forms of creation.

Some masters devote themselves to weapons and protective equipment. They study the strength of materials, the balance of components, and the qualities needed for a combatant to use their equipment effectively. The enchantments they create can improve the properties of a weapon or a suit of armour, according to the effects provided by the spell lists they have mastered.

Others favour stone, metal, or natural substances. They learn to modify certain properties of matter and employ their power to bring about transformations that ordinary methods could not achieve.

Gems hold an important place in several Elven traditions. Cutting them requires detailed knowledge of their structure, while their transparency and natural qualities can contribute to the creation of particularly remarkable objects.

Liquids and gaseous substances offer other possibilities. Some Herutanor study preparations, solutions, and potions whose effects depend upon a precise combination of ingredients and magical powers.

Imbedding is a distinct discipline. It makes it possible to fix certain spells within objects so that their effects may be used in accordance with the applicable rules. Designing such works requires an understanding of activation conditions, the duration of enchantments, and the limitations specific to each spell list.

Creation also demands constant attention to the future use of an object. A protective item intended for a traveller must suit the demands of a journey. An object designed to remain in a chamber for several centuries presents different requirements.

The Herutano thus learns to consider a work as a whole. They must understand its materials, the effects sought, and the circumstances in which those effects will be employed.

The beauty of a creation remains important, but its worth also depends upon its usefulness, its strength, and the responsibilities its creator is willing to assume.

Healing and Self-Mastery

The profession possesses a feature that distinguishes it from many other craft traditions: some of its disciplines directly concern healing and bodily faculties.

Meditative Healing allows the practitioner to employ inner mastery to act upon certain kinds of physical harm. Its effects may concern their own body and, depending on the spells available, those of other people.

This skill plays an important part in a craftsman's life.

Working with metals, stones, and precision instruments involves risks. Hand injuries, burns, and accidents can seriously compromise a master's ability to continue their work.

Magical healing may then supplement ordinary care, within the limitations of the spells mastered.

It also has considerable value during travel. A Herutano accompanying a company may help an injured companion even when their principal expertise remains craftsmanship.

Instruction in this discipline nevertheless demands careful attention to the body's limits. Concentration and self-mastery do not replace the examination of injuries, rest, or the knowledge needed to recognise conditions beyond the character's powers.

The ability to act upon certain bodily functions contributes, finally, to the distinctive character of the Herutano's Mentalism. It links inner discipline to material creation, within a tradition where precision of thought accompanies precision of movement.

The Last Dwellings of the Craftsmen

After the destruction of Eregion, the craft traditions of the Eldar survive in several regions of Middle-earth.

At Imladris, survivors of the ancient wars preserve knowledge and objects, some dating back to the vanished realms. The workshops may be devoted to repairing precious works, preserving manuscripts, or making objects for inhabitants and travellers.

In Lindon, the Elves maintain other traditions. The Grey Havens are home to craftsmen whose expertise may concern ships, the materials required for their upkeep, and objects intended for those undertaking the voyage into the West.

The woodland realms likewise possess their own practices. The craftsmen of Lórien work with materials suited to their surroundings, and some of their creations display qualities that foreign travellers find remarkable.

These traditions do not imply that every Elven object possesses an enchantment in the RMU sense. Exceptional mastery of a craft can produce works that seem extraordinary without necessarily involving a spell list.

A Herutano may nevertheless contribute to these activities by combining magical knowledge with the techniques of other craftsmen.

In the Third Age, the gradual decline of the Elven realms gives their responsibilities a new dimension. Ancient works become witnesses to times that few peoples can still remember directly.

Some masters choose to pass their knowledge to the young. Others seek to restore damaged works or preserve objects that will accompany their people into the West.

The departure of the Elves profoundly changes the destiny of their creations. An object long kept in a dwelling may be entrusted to a companion, offered to a mortal friend, or left in the care of a community that understands its importance.

These decisions give the Herutano a particular relationship with the passage of time and with those to whom they wish to entrust their works.

The Creator's Pride and the Shadow

The pursuit of perfection is one of the most powerful aspirations of great craftsmen. It encourages patience, study, and the desire to deepen inherited knowledge.

Yet this ambition can also lead to dangerous decisions.

A Herutano may devote several decades to a creation and refuse to acknowledge its flaws. They may seek to preserve a work whose loss seems unbearable or grow increasingly jealous of another master's achievements.

The history of Fëanor and that of the smiths of Eregion give these tensions considerable weight.

The Silmarils attest to extraordinary mastery, but their history is marked by possessiveness and by the oaths sworn after their theft. The Rings of Power, meanwhile, arise from a desire to preserve and enhance, before the teachings of Annatar reveal their true peril.

A Herutano character may face more modest temptations whose consequences nevertheless remain significant.

A stranger offers a method capable of greatly improving their enchantments but refuses to explain its origin. A patron asks them to create an object that could be used against innocent people. An ancient manuscript reveals a technique whose effects go beyond anything taught during their apprenticeship.

The craftsman must then decide how far to pursue their research.

The profession thus offers an especially rich setting for exploring the Shadow and Corruption. The risks depend on the nature of the powers employed and the deeds performed, in accordance with MERP-RMU mechanics.

A Herutano may seek personal renown, the protection of a dwelling, or the preservation of a precious memory. Their intentions deserve to be understood, but they do not render their chosen means harmless.

The true difficulty often arises when the character must abandon a creation they consider essential.

Leaving the Workshop

A Herutano may have devoted much of their life to working in a single dwelling. Journeys then take on particular importance, carrying them far from the materials, instruments, and knowledge to which they are accustomed.

Some set out in search of an ancient object. A work attributed to a vanished master has been discovered among the ruins, but its properties remain unknown. A fragment of a manuscript mentions a method whose last traces lead towards a region abandoned for several centuries.

Others wish to find a companion or honour a commitment.

A Herutano who survived the destruction of Eregion may search for an apprentice who disappeared during the war. A craftsman of Imladris undertakes a journey to return a weapon to the family of its former owner. A master of the Grey Havens accompanies travellers to a dwelling where an ancient work needs repair.

Life within a company allows them to use their skills in unfamiliar circumstances.

They may identify the composition of an object, examine inscriptions, help repair equipment, or assist their companions in understanding the effects of an enchantment.

Their knowledge becomes especially valuable when travellers discover the remains of ancient civilisations.

Among the ruins of Eregion, Gondolin, or the realms of the Dwarves, a Herutano may recognise a craftsman's hand, identify a material, or understand the principles of a method of manufacture unknown to their companions.

Yet adventure also obliges them to develop other skills.

The roads become difficult, resources run short, and certain dangers demand swift decisions. The character then discovers the value of companions whose training differs from their own.

A Ranger teaches them to travel through the wild lands; a Fighter shows them the practical demands placed upon the weapons they make; a Razak-Zinul may reveal methods of working metal they have never encountered before.

These exchanges gradually enrich their experience and remind them that great works often arise from shared knowledge.

Playing a Herutano

The Herutano offers the opportunity to portray an Elf whose existence is deeply connected to creation, memory, and the transmission of knowledge.

A young Noldo may have left their workshop to complete an apprenticeship under a renowned master. A Sindarin craftswoman seeks to restore an object preserved since the wars of the First Age. A survivor of Eregion continues research interrupted by the destruction of their realm, while an Elf of the Grey Havens prepares the last works they wish to finish before leaving Middle-earth.

The character's cultural origins determine their relationship with craftsmanship.

A Noldo may retain a profound admiration for the masters of Valinor. A Sinda possesses traditions shaped by the realms of Beleriand and by relations with neighbouring peoples. A Silvan Elf may favour the materials of the forest and the objects needed by their community.

The relationship with their master remains essential.

Who first taught them their skills? What creation marked the completion of their apprenticeship? Is there a method they have never managed to understand, or an object whose creation they now regret?

The Herutano's personality may be shaped by the demands of their art.

Some masters develop great patience, accustomed to reworking their creations until they achieve a satisfactory result. Others become particularly exacting towards their disciples, convinced that passing on knowledge imperfectly understood can have lasting consequences.

The length of an Elven life also lends unusual depth to their relationships.

A craftsman may keep a tool given to them by a companion who died centuries ago. A gem remains associated with the memory of a destroyed dwelling, while an unfinished work recalls a master whose teachings continue to influence their research.

Such memories may nourish their desire to create, but they may also prevent them from accepting the world's transformations.

Over the course of their adventures, the Herutano must decide what they wish to preserve and what they can allow to pass away. Their talents enable them to fashion exceptional works; their relationships with others give meaning to the creations they choose to undertake.

Gamemaster's Notes — The Herutano in MERP-RMU

The Herutano is a pure Mentalism spell user, specialising in the creation of objects, the transformation of matter, and magical imbedding.

In the historical reference rules, this profession is restricted to Elven cultures.

Prime Stats

Its prime stats are Presence (Pr) and Self Discipline (SD).

Presence supports the faculties associated with the realm of Mentalism, while Self Discipline represents the concentration and inner mastery required for its enchantments.

The Herutano and Other Magical Craftsmen

The Herutano uses Mentalism. Their enchantments rely on profound mastery of the mind and on the interaction of their powers with objects.

The Razak-Zinul belongs to the traditions of the Khazâd and practises Channeling. Their knowledge concerns, in particular, the works, inscriptions, and craft methods of their people.

The Alchemist is an Essence user whose spell lists provide more general training in transformations and enchantments.

These professions may pursue similar goals, but their realms of magic, traditions, and spell lists remain distinct.

The Fëa and the Art of the Eldar

The association between the fëa and matter provides a way to represent, through MERP-RMU mechanics, the Elves' particular relationship with their creations.

It is an interpretation for the game and must not be presented as an exhaustive explanation of Elven magic in Tolkien's writings.

The Herutanor possess no general power allowing them to divide, fragment, or transfer their souls into objects.

Exceptional Works

The Silmarils, the Rings of Power, and Tolkien's other great creations belong to unique events in the history of Arda.

They serve as literary references for portraying the traditions of craftsmen, but must not be treated as objects a character could automatically create simply by developing a spell list.

The Gamemaster thus preserves the distinction between creations available to characters under RMU and the exceptional works whose nature exceeds the game's ordinary mechanics.

Shadow and Corruption

The profession has no intrinsic association with the Shadow.

Risks arise when the character uses corrupted powers, seeks unjustified domination, or accepts teachings whose nature falls under the Shadow and Corruption mechanics established by MERP-RMU.

The history of Fëanor and that of the craftsmen of Eregion provide important references for exploring pride, possessiveness, and the temptation to preserve things at the cost of another's freedom.

The Gamemaster must nevertheless distinguish ordinary moral failings from events that actually produce mechanical Corruption consequences.

The Herutano comes fully into its own when portrayed as a master craftsman whose mastery of matter, inner discipline, and sense of responsibility determine the nature of the works they will leave behind.
